By Mike Allen · Nov 16, 2026

☀️ Good Monday morning! Smart Brevity™ count: 1,624 words ... 6 mins. Thanks to Noah Bressner for orchestrating. Edited by Bill Kole.

⚡ Ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is considering a far-fetched comeback bid, with one ally planning a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to build support, including lobbying the White House, the Financial Times reports.

✈️ Driving the day: President Trump today begins a four-day Asia swing that'll take him through Alaska to Manila, the Philippines. Then he heads for Shenzhen, the Silicon Valley of China, where he'll hold a rare trilateral summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin to discuss nuclear stockpiles.
 
 
1 big thing: Shock and awe, forever
 

Illustration: Annelise Capossela/Axios
 

It was random, but related, that we were hit with a tectonic election result, an epic AI-and-spy scandal, and the dramatic FAA shutdown in just over one week, Jim VandeHei and Mike Allen write in a "Behind the Curtain" column.

  • This is our new reality: constant shock and awe, igniting chain reactions across politics, media, AI, business and culture.

Why it matters: This month's three shocks hit separately. But their speed and spread are our new reality.

Politics, AI, media and business are now one wired system: A jolt in one sets off the other three, instantly.

  • We call this post-processable velocity: Change is moving faster than any person, company, market or government can absorb.

What makes all this so disorienting for all of us is how interconnected politics, AI, business and media have become. The Nvidia spy scandal is a vivid example:

  • Media, last weekend: The New York Times reports that Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned President Trump that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang was tied to a suspected Chinese spy. Social media erupts.
  • Business, Monday: Nvidia stock falls more than 4% at the open and keeps sliding. Fears of economy-wide AI fallout follow.
  • Politics, all week: Trump's top team gets dragged into a "what did they know and when" frenzy. Democrats demand hearings.
  • Policy, now: Lawmakers are scrambling to untangle the web of spies, lies and AI, and are racing to tighten China's access to Nvidia chips that gave Huang the power he's now surrendered.
  • Tech, going forward: AI companies are rethinking their reliance on Nvidia chips and exploring financing options beyond Nvidia.

Three forces make this permanent:

🔄 1. Politics swings wildly. This was the seventh straight election in which the White House, Senate or House changed hands. And this time, in truly unthinkable and historic ways.

  • There were a number of "split districts" in 2024 that went for Kamala Harris for president and a Republican for the House. This year, every single one swung to electing a Democrat. We can't find any precedent for this.
  • It's possible we've hit a post-ideological age where people feel very little affiliation to party tribes. How do you explain young men shifting almost 40 points from Republicans to Democrats in two years?

🤖 2. AI concentrates everything. A handful of companies are making historic bets on superhuman intelligence, and propping up the economy while they do it.

  • That puts enormous power and risk in very few hands. One man's affair shook the whole market.
  • Nvidia makes the vital ingredient of AI, and helps finance nearly every big player buying it.

⛓️‍💥 3. Everything is fragile when everything is interconnected. Friday's flight shutdown had nothing to do with AI, spies or elections, but it still shook us all.

  • It appears a contractor was swapping copper wire for fiber. Routers overloaded. Departures stopped nationwide for more than four hours.
  • A total of 18,000+ U.S. flights were canceled over the past three days.

The bottom line: The shocks will change. The speed won't.

2. 🗳️ Dems' unlikely plan: Make Trump look good
 

Photo illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Photo: Alex Wong/Getty Images
 

Holly Otterbein — co-author of our weekly Axios 2028 newsletter — writes from the What's Next summit, a gathering of centrist Dems in Denver:

Democrats' euphoria over their once-in-a-generation wave of midterm victories is giving way to a reality check:

  • They were lucky to have a weakened opposition. And they might be "renting" this year's voters if they don't quickly deliver on their promises.

Why it matters: If Democrats want to rack up policy wins ASAP, they'll need to work with President Trump — the guy many of them held up as what's wrong with America. That means giving him a few wins.

🔬 Zoom in: Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico argued exactly that late last week at the What's Next summit.

  • "If President Trump wants the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality," Talarico said. "We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history."
  • Gina Hinojosa, who'll be Texas' first Democratic governor in more than three decades, has said she'll work with Trump on immigration. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, a frequent Trump target, is pitching the president on rebranding Medicare for All as "TrumpCare" to get it passed.
  • On CNN's "State of the Union" yesterday, Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom told Dana Bash he wants to collaborate with Trump to deliver on the president's own past promise to lower grocery prices.

🔭 Zoom out: Some top Democrats are determined not to repeat the mistakes the party made after the 2022 elections, when they overperformed — and grew complacent. They lost the presidential election two years later.

3. 👀 MAGA pushes Trump-tech divorce
 

Photo illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Photo: Nicholas Kamm/AFP via Getty Images
 

Prominent conservative thinkers and MAGA figures are seizing on Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy to pull President Trump away from his alliance with the tech right, Axios' Maria Curi writes.

  • These right-wing players view the midterm elections as proof that people across the political spectrum hate AI and data centers, and view Silicon Valley as too powerful.

Oren Cass, founder of conservative think tank American Compass, said Trump's perception of China "has always been entirely commercial and transactional. His view was: 'We're getting screwed. I'm going to get a better deal.'"

  • Cass, who has warned about Nvidia risks for more than a year, said the allegations of espionage are the strongest evidence yet that China isn't a commercial partner but an adversary that is going to "subvert the American political process in ways that end up humiliating the President."

4. 🤖 Charted: Retail traders buy Nvidia dip
 
Data: FactSet. Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

Everyday investors piled into Nvidia after Jensen Huang's resignation and helped soften the blow to its stock, Axios' Matt Phillips writes.

  • Why it matters: The rush to "buy the dip" shows some investors still believe in the AI boom.

🧮 By the numbers: About 5.1 million call options on Nvidia — bets that its stock will rise — traded Thursday after Huang's resignation was announced.

  • That's the second-highest single-day total this year.

5. 🩺 Insurance hikes hit companies hard
 

Illustration: Annelise Capossela/Axios
 

Double-digit premium hikes have hit more than a third of companies renewing their health insurance plans, Axios' Adriel Bettelheim writes from a new Gallagher survey of more than 3,700 firms.

  • Why it matters: When costs spike for employers, workers feel it through smaller raises, higher out-of-pocket costs or skimpier coverage.

Zoom in: Cancer care is the No. 1 cost driver for about 7 in 10 firms.

  • Keep reading.
 
 
6. 🏛️ Administration threatens to prosecute Dems
 

Via X
 

White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller tweeted support yesterday after a federal prosecutor accused Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, of intending to "weaponize congressional investigations."

  • Why it matters: The Trump administration, with a series of such letters to House and Senate Democrats, is preemptively warning Democrats, seven weeks before they take over the House and Senate, that the Justice Department could consider overly aggressive "congressional investigations and subpoenas" to be a crime.

The prosecutor, U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz of Houston, ordered Warren to preserve "all potentially relevant evidence related to your efforts to suppress associational activities related to President Trump and the Trump Administration," for potential use in a conspiracy case.

  • "Failure to do so ... may carry significant legal consequences," Reitz said.

Reitz argued in a two-page letter to Warren that her comments in post-midterm interviews suggest she will "target private individuals close to President Trump." Reitz added: "The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them."

  • Reitz told The Wall Street Journal: "We don't have to wait for them to commit a crime for us to begin investigating whether there's a basis to escalate or indict or prosecute ... [Democrats] are champing at the bit with bloodlust to punish those who associate with the president."

Reality check: The Constitution grants lawmakers legal immunity for legislative actions.
 
 
7. 🌊 California's monster waves
 
People run as waves crash onto Beach Boulevard in Pacifica, Calif., near San Francisco on Saturday. Photo: Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle via AP

Huge waves — the biggest in nearly two years — pummeled the California coast over the weekend, inundating beaches and flooding local streets.

  • Waves over 50 feet were recorded in San Mateo County, just south of San Francisco, on Saturday.
Crowds gather to watch big waves and surfers at Mavericks Beach in Half Moon Bay, Calif., on Saturday. Photo: Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images

In Southern California, iconic piers in Ventura, Manhattan Beach, Huntington Beach and San Diego's Pacific Beach were closed.

  • The ongoing super El Niño — an unusually strong warming of Pacific waters — has raised coastal sea levels as warmer water expands and ocean currents shift, potentially allowing waves to push farther inland.

8. 🦃 1 fun thing: The 100th parade
 
From left: Megan Moroney, Keke Palmer, Queen Latifah and Teddy Swims. Image: AP

Megan Moroney, Teddy Swims, Queen Latifah, Keke Palmer, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots and Smash Mouth will be part of the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, stepping off in 10 days.

  • The lineup includes a record-breaking 100 aerial balloons, including Bluey, Mickey Mouse and Hello Kitty.

📺 Fun fact: The 2½-mile parade has become such a tradition while we prep our turkeys that NBC's coverage ranks each year among the top 100 most-watched telecasts.

  • The parade begins on NBC at 8:30 a.m. on Thanksgiving Day in all time zones and will feature a tribute to Dolly Parton led by actress and singer Megan Hilty, AP reports.
  • The familiar hosts — Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb and Al Roker from the "Today" show — will return on NBC and Peacock, with coverage running until noon.
